This experiment does not show that "thoughts are data". It shows that, in a particular species of well-researched snail, pain stimulus causes a chemical change in their neurons' nuclei, and you can reproduce that chemical change in another snail.

Things it does not show:

  • Humans store memories in the neuron nucleus

  • Humans can have memories extracted

  • Humans can have memories implanted

We still have NO, repeat NO, idea where or how the human brain stores memories, how to extract them, or how to implant them. But we can kinda do a similar thing with snails.

No, there's more. The reason this won't work in humans is because we have brains with space for memory, and snails don't. They literally don't have the neuron real estate to hold memories. 20,000 neurons vs. 1 billion neurons.

Our memories are stored as vast (but tiny) clouds in our brains, and multiple emotional areas are tied to them, like anger or happiness. There's no way to "extract" that "data", our brains are more like analog sponges than digital webs.

Snails don't have that luxury, they have a small ganglion (nerve cluster) in the head that mostly controls the eyes and mouth. They need their foot nerves to store memories, because the ganglion is busy with the eyes. So am I surprised their nuclei change composition after repeated painful stimuli? No. It's the only "memory" they have.

But humans just don't work that way. You can't extract hand nerves and implant them in my hand and whoa, now I can shoot a gun with perfect accuracy. We're more complicated than snails.
